sweep_summary: Bunun (bunu1267) is in the catalog as set by morphology on De Busser 2009 (Takivatan: penultimate stress counted on the root, only focus -un/-an shift it). the list of works with stress in the title had one item, Huang 2008 (Linguistics 46.1, Isbukun + Takituduh dialects): relevant to word stress, but paywalled at De Gruyter with no open copy anywhere checked (Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, CORE, OpenAlex, Academia Sinica Scholars Hub, the Internet Archive, researchgate/thefreelibrary bot pages); its abstract (OpenAlex) says Isbukun has unmarked penultimate stress that shifts to final position when a heavy syllable would otherwise be in weak position, and Takituduh keeps disyllabic feet, i.e. the same base-penult rule plus quantity sensitivity, so it refines the record (weight fields) rather than the classification; priority high to acquire. Two extra first-hand sources were read: (1) Ouyang 2012 'Stress and Suffixation in Isbukun Bunun' (Coyote Papers 20, pp. 100-108), recovered from the the Internet Archive since repository.arizona.edu could not be reached by automated download; it states for Isbukun a single right-edge moraic trochee (final heavy = long vowel/diphthong stressed, else penultimate; codas weightless; no secondary stress) with inflectional suffixes and clitics never stressed and derivational suffixes (-un/-an etc.) shifting stress rightward. This is the best new statement: it confirms the morphological classification for a second dialect and refines the catalog's 'what counts as heavy: not-applicable' as Takivatan-only, but does not supersede the deciding thesis. (2) De Busser's 2011 NTHU handout (already held by the project; URL confirmed at rdbusser.com/), sec. 3.5, restates the thesis rule verbatim in substance and confirms the catalog. A Brill Handbook of Formosan Languages 'Bunun' chapter (De Busser & Li, doi:10.1163/2772-5766_hflo_com_305050) exists but is paywalled and unread (priority medium). All downloads and metadata records are and listed in there. searching was done through OpenAlex, Crossref, Semantic Scholar, Unpaywall, CORE, the Internet Archive and direct downloads.

new_statements.quote: In Isbukun Bunun, coda consonants do not contribute to syllable weight. Syllables with a long vowel (CV:C) or diphthong (CVVC) are heavy, and syllables with a short vowel (CVC) are light. A single quantity-sensitive trochee is formed at the right edge of a word (Huang 2008), as shown in (1). (1) a. Stress falls on the final syllable if it is heavy. L(ˈH)# si.la.(ˈla:) 'provoke; challenge' H(ˈH)# ma.aun.(ˈvai) 'win in arm wrestling' b. If the final syllable is light, stress falls on the penultimate syllable. (ˈLL)# pi.(ˈnas.kal) 'make happy' (ˈH)L# i.(ˈais).ku 'near to'
new_statements.citation: Ouyang, Iris Chuoying. 2012. Stress and Suffixation in Isbukun Bunun. Coyote Papers 20 (University of Arizona Linguistics Circle), pp. 100-108. hdl:10150/253425 (Internet Archive copy 2024-09-26 of the repository.arizona.edu bitstream).
new_statements.reading: Isbukun Bunun (a different dialect from the catalog's Takivatan): one right-edge moraic trochee; final syllable stressed if heavy (long vowel or diphthong; codas weightless), otherwise penultimate; no secondary stress. Morphological conditioning as in Takivatan: derivational suffixes (incl. focus -un/-an) are inside the stress domain and pull stress rightward, inflectional suffixes (-in, -aŋ), determiners and pronominal clitics are never stressed and leave base stress in place (sec. 2.4, 2.6: 'inflectional suffixes and clitics are never stressed'). So the catalog's set by morphology classification holds for Isbukun too, but the record's weight fields ('what counts as heavy: not-applicable', vowel length non-phonemic) are Takivatan-specific: Isbukun is quantity-sensitive (long vowel / diphthong = heavy) with the same base-penult default. This is the first-hand Isbukun statement the catalog flagged as unreached.

sources.quote: 'Most words in Bunun have penultimate stress on the word root. This means that stress falls on the second-to-last syllable of the form that remains when you take away all the affixes. qaisiŋ [ˈqai.sɪŋ], baluku [ba.ˈlu.ku], haðun-in [ˈha.ðu.nin] (stress is not changed by the suffix -in). Some affixes do change the stress, such as the undergoer focus suffix -un and the locative focus suffix -an. liskin [ˈlɪʃ.kɪn] (penultimate) but: in-liskin-an [ɪn.lɪʃ.ˈkiː.nan] (last root syllable)'
sources.note: Same author and same rule as the catalog's deciding source (De Busser 2009 thesis): penultimate stress counted on the root with affixes stripped; -in and other affixes invisible; -un/-an shift stress rightward. Stated for 'Bunun' in a handout that covers Takivatan and Isbukun, but the examples are the Takivatan ones from the thesis; no weight statement.

sources.note: An Autosegmental-Metrical study of prosodic structure and intonational phonology of Bunun (and 12 other Formosan languages) from original fieldwork; finds that Formosan languages 'show rich tonal phonologies in their intonational systems' with complex stress-morphology interactions, and specifically that 'Bunun has distinct pitch accent melodies for words vs. clitics' - i.e. post-lexical (intonational) pitch accents anchored to word stress, not lexical tone. This is the only first-hand tonal (F0/pitch accent) analysis of Bunun located by S or C.

tone.quote: タキバカ方言において，アクセントは次末モーラを含む音節にアクセントに置かれる。(C)VCV(C) の音節構造を持つ語では語末音節，次末音節とも母音1つを含むので，次末モーラは次末音節に含まれる。そのため次末音節にアクセントが落ちる。（1）に例を挙げる。左は接尾辞の付かない形式，右は一音節から成る接尾辞 -an（非動作主態・場所主語）または -un（非動作主態・対象主語）の付いた形式である。接尾辞自体 1モーラを持っているので，接尾辞が付くと，次末モーラは語根・語幹の最終音節に含まれることになる。そのため，接尾辞が付くとアクセントが右に移動する。（1） maludaq [ma.ˈlu.daq] ludaq-an [lu.ˈɗa.qan] 「打つ」 kalat [ˈka.lat] kalat-un [ka.ˈlat.un] 「噛む」
tone.locator: p. 35, sec. 1 「タキバカ方言のアクセント」 (with Table 1 'ブヌン語方言のアクセント型', p. 34)
tone.translation: In the Takibakha dialect, the accent is placed on the syllable that contains the penultimate mora. In words of (C)VCV(C) structure both the final and the penultimate syllable contain one vowel, so the penultimate mora lies in the penultimate syllable; hence the accent falls on the penultimate syllable. Examples are given in (1): on the left the unsuffixed form, on the right the form with the monosyllabic suffix -an (non-actor voice, locative subject) or -un (non-actor voice, patient subject). Since the suffix itself carries one mora, once it is attached the penultimate mora comes to lie in the last syllable of the root/stem; therefore the accent moves to the right under suffixation. (1) maludaq [ma.ˈlu.daq] : ludaq-an [lu.ˈɗa.qan] 'hit'; kalat [ˈka.lat] : kalat-un [ka.ˈlat.un] 'bite'.

sources.note: From over 240 first-hand loanword items, the paper finds that Japanese loanwords in Isbukun Bunun ignore the Japanese accent and take stress by the native Bunun rules, except that closed syllables, light in native words, attract stress in loans (and lose that weight after a bimoraic syllable). The catalog entry codes the Takivatan dialect from De Busser 2009 (penultimate stress on the root, morphological), so this adds Isbukun loanword detail (a coda-weight effect confined to loans) without giving a main stress position that could confirm or contradict the entry.

tone.says: First formal analysis (240+ first-hand items) of how Japanese loanwords are prosodically adapted in Isbukun Bunun: the position of the Japanese (pitch) accent is entirely disregarded and stress is assigned by native Bunun rules, except that closed syllables, light in native phonology, attract stress in loans (and may become light again after a bimoraic syllable); analysed as variable ranking of a moraic-coda constraint against a constraint penalizing unstressed heavies. I.e. Bunun word prosody…
